title: Post CXX Annos Patebo: the Cloister, Damcar, Fez, and the Vault of Seven Sides
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Germany, the birth the Confessio dates and does not place
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Confessio Fraternitatis (1615) states the year 1378 and no external record of any kind corroborates it; month and day default to 01-01
stops.campa: In a Germany the manifestos never name, no town, no province, no river, a son is born to a noble family whose fortune is gone. The Confessio gives the year and nothing else: 1378. No parish register holds him, no chronicle of the Empire records the house. Every later map that plants his cradle in a specific German town is drawing on fraternal invention two centuries downstream. The canon supplies a date and a blank where the place should be. A founder without a birthplace can be claimed by any country that wants him.
stops.quote: from the year of our Lord 1378. (in which year our Christian Father was born) till now
suggested_refs: The geographic centroid of Germany, standing in for a birthplace neither manifesto names
sources: Confessio Fraternitatis (1615), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: A cloister in Germany, placed in the fifth year of age
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Fama gives an age, not a year; 1383 is arithmetic from the Confessio's 1378
stops.campa: By reason of his poverty, though descended of noble parents, the boy is placed in a cloister in the fifth year of his age. The monks teach him Greek and Latin, indifferently, which is the Fama's own word for it. No house is named, no rule, no abbot. The cause of the placement is money, not death. The Greek and the Latin are the whole of what the house gives him, and he will go to Arabia for the rest. Later retellings say he was orphaned at four and kept twelve years; the manifesto says neither orphan, nor four, nor any duration at all.
stops.quote: in the fifth year of age was placed in a Cloyster, where had learned indifferently the Greek and Latin Tongues
suggested_refs: The unnamed cloister of the Fama, later the recruiting ground for the first three brethren
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Southern Germany, setting out with Brother P.A.L.
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Fama dates the departure only as 'being yet in his growing years' and gives no age; the pin is a route inference, not a stated place
stops.campa: Still in his growing years, he is joined to a brother of the house called only P.A.L., who has determined to go to the Holy Land. The two set out from Germany for Jerusalem. The Fama names no road, no port, no season, and gives the boy no age for the leaving; the sixteen years that later summaries attach to this departure belong further down the page, to his arrival in Arabia. Two initials and a destination are the whole of the record. The pin sits in southern Germany because the road to the Mediterranean ran that way, not because a text says so.
stops.quote: being yet in his growing years, was associated to a Brother, P.A.L. who had determined to go to the Holy Land
suggested_refs: The overland pilgrim routes from the Empire to the Adriatic and Levantine ports
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

segments.name: The Road That Does Not Reach Jerusalem

stops.name: Cyprus, the death of Brother P.A.L.
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama names the island and no date; the year is arithmetic from the chronology of the journey
stops.campa: Brother P.A.L. dies in Cyprus and never comes to Jerusalem. The manifesto names the island and stops: no town, no church, no grave, no cause. Later tradition proposes Famagusta, the Lusignan port through which the pilgrim traffic of the age passed, and the proposal is convenient rather than attested. The boy does not turn back. He is alone now, on a journey undertaken for another man's vow, in a sea he has never seen. His only credential is the initials of a dead companion.
stops.quote: Although this Brother dyed in Ciprus, and so never came to Jerusalem, yet our Brother C.R. did not return
suggested_refs: Famagusta and the Lusignan pilgrim ports of Cyprus, proposed by tradition and unsupported by the text
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Sepulchre never reached
stops.date_confidence: not a visit: this is the stated destination of the journey, and the Fama is explicit that he never arrives
stops.campa: Jerusalem is the reason the journey began and the thing P.A.L. died chasing. Christian Rosenkreuz does not reach it. He ships himself to Damascus meaning to go on from there, and the going on never happens. The Sepulchre stands in this list as the one stop on the route that stays empty: named in the text, fixed on the map, never entered by the traveller. He finds the Arabian sages, the vault and the order instead, and the legend will claim all three as the point of the journey.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, destination of the vow that started the journey
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Damascus, the feebleness of the body
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama gives the city and the reason for the stay, no date
stops.campa: He reaches Damascus intending Jerusalem, and the feebleness of his body keeps him there. He cures the sick by his skill in physick and wins much favour with the Turks, and in the meantime hears of wise men living further off. This is the pin Ibn Arabi crosses in 1223 and dies on in 1240, buried at the foot of Mount Qasiyun; the same city Rene Guenon's Shadhili initiation chain runs back to; the region where Molay's file puts the Mamluk and Mongol armies at Shaqhab in 1303. The atlas has been here long before him.
stops.quote: he shipped himself over, and went to Damasco, minding from thence to go to Jerusalem; but by reason of the feebleness of his body he remained still there
suggested_refs: The Damascus pin inherited byte-identical from ibn_arabi.journey.json and rene_guenon.journey.json
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Damcar, received not as a stranger
stops.date_confidence: legendary: place identified with Dhamar in Yemen by later commentators only; the Fama says 'Damasco in Arabia' and the Confessio says 'the City Damear in Arabia'
stops.campa: He goes on to the city of the sages. They receive him not as a stranger but as one whom they had long expected, and they call him by his name, and they tell him things out of his own cloister that he had thought no one knew. He is sixteen years old on arrival, of a strong Dutch constitution, and he has come to a place the manifesto sets in Arabia without ever saying how far. A pilgrim who lost his companion on the road has become, in one sentence, a man who was awaited.
stops.quote: there the Wise received him (as he himself witnesseth) not as a stranger, but as one whom they had long expected, they called him by his name
suggested_refs: Dhamar, Yemen, the identification later commentators propose for Damcar
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource
Wikipedia summary of Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972)

stops.name: Damcar, the Book M into good Latin
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama dates the translation to 'the year following' his arrival and gives no absolute year
stops.campa: The year following his arrival he has the Arabian tongue well enough to turn the Book M into good Latin, and he carries that translation back to Europe with him. The manifesto writes two characters, Book M, and never expands them; Liber M and Book of the World are later commentary sold as text. Whatever M holds, the Fama treats it as the physical proof of the journey, an object rather than a doctrine, the one thing brought out of Arabia that a European scholar could be made to open and read.
stops.quote: He learned there better the Arabian Tongue; so that the year following he translated the Book M. into good Latin
suggested_refs: The Book M, named by initial only in the Fama and never described
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Damcar, three years of physick and the mathematics
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the three-year span is stated in the Fama; the terminal year is arithmetic
stops.campa: Three years he studies at Damcar, and what he studies is physick and the mathematics, not physics; the sages' instruments answer questions Europe has not yet learned to ask. Kabbalah and magic belong to Fez, later, and get moved here by careless summary. The place-name itself will not hold still: the Fama's English calls the sages men of Damasco in Arabia, folding them into the Syrian city, while the Confessio calls their home Damear. Yates reads Damcar; the two manifestos were never reconciled with each other.
stops.quote: This is the place where he did learn his Physick, and his Mathematicks
suggested_refs: The unresolved Damasco / Damear split between the two manifestos in Vaughan's English
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource
Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972), via Wikipedia

segments.name: Sinus Arabicus, Egypt, Fez, and the Rejection in Spain

stops.name: The Red Sea, shipped over Sinus Arabicus
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama names the sea and neither shore; this coordinate is deliberately mid-water and asserts no harbour
stops.campa: With good consent he takes his leave and ships himself over Sinus Arabicus into Egypt. The Fama gives the sea and neither shore: no port of embarkation, no port of landing, no ship, no season. This pin floats in open water on purpose, midway between the Egyptian and Arabian coasts, because setting it at Al-Qusayr or any other harbour would assert a harbour the text refuses to name. He is perhaps twenty years old and carries a Latin manuscript out of a country whose sages knew his name before he did.
stops.quote: After three years he returned again with good consent, shipped himself over Sinus Arabicus into Egypt, where he remained not long
suggested_refs: The Arabia-to-Egypt trade crossing of the Red Sea, unnamed on both shores in the manifesto
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Egypt, the plants and the creatures
stops.date_confidence: legendary: no city and no duration beyond 'remained not long'; Cairo is a placeholder the text does not authorise
stops.campa: He does not remain long in Egypt. Long enough to take better notice of the plants and the creatures, which is all the manifesto says he does there, and then he is gone. No city, no temple, no pyramid, no teacher. The whole Egyptian episode occupies one clause. Cairo carries the pin only as the obvious centre of any Egypt a traveller crossed in 1397, and stands here as a placeholder rather than a stop. The legend that will later be read as Hermetic and Egyptian to its roots barely stops in Egypt.
suggested_refs: Cairo as conventional stand-in for the Fama's unnamed Egypt
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Fez, the Elementary Inhabitants
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama gives a two-year stay at Fez and no dates; the pin is the atlas's existing Fez coordinate
stops.campa: The Arabians of Damcar direct him to Fez, and he sails the whole Mediterranean to reach it. Two years he stays. He gets acquainted with those the text calls the Elementary Inhabitants, who reveal to him many of their secrets, and he studies the mathematica, physic and magic in which the men of Fez are most skilful. Ibn Arabi settles in this city in 1195 after his parents die; Maimonides shelters here from 1160 to 1165 disguised as a Muslim. The manifesto records no teacher's name and no place of lodging for either year.
stops.quote: he sailed over the whole Mediterranean Sea for to come unto Fez, where the Arabians had directed him
suggested_refs: The al-Qarawiyyin quarter of Fez; pin inherited byte-identical from ibn_arabi.journey.json
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Fez, the Magia not altogether pure
stops.date_confidence: legendary: end of the stated two years, no year in the text
stops.campa: What he finally objects to at Fez is not their competence but their creed: their Magia, he says, was not altogether pure, and their Cabala defiled with their religion. The manifesto never rates Fez below Damcar; it rates the men of Fez most skilful of all in the three arts, and then has him leave anyway. He is not gathering the best available magic; he is sorting a mixed inheritance, and the sorting is done on Christian grounds. Two years at Fez leave him with a criterion rather than a doctrine.
stops.quote: their Magia was not altogether pure, and also that their Cabala was defiled with their Religion
suggested_refs: The Fama's doctrinal test applied at Fez, the order's first act of selection
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Tangier, sailing with many costly things
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no port of departure is named in the Fama; the Strait crossing is the plain route and the pin is a route inference
stops.campa: After two years he departs the city of Fez and sails with many costly things into Spain. The manifesto counts no chests and names no port; a crossing from the Moroccan Atlantic or the Strait is the plain route and not a stated one, so the pin sits at Tangier, where Ibn Arabi makes his last crossing out of al-Andalus in 1196 going the other way. Christian Rosenkreuz is carrying books, instruments and a translation, and he believes Europe is waiting for them. Nothing has yet told him what Europe does with a man who arrives holding corrections.
stops.quote: After two years Brother C. R. departed the City Fez, and sailed with many costly things into Spain
suggested_refs: The Strait of Gibraltar crossing, also the 1196 exit point in ibn_arabi.journey.json
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Spain, the reformation laughed at
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the manifesto names no Spanish city and no year; Toledo is a later guess and carries the pin only as that
stops.campa: In Spain he lays before the learned what he has brought: the errors in their arts, the corrections, the reformation of the whole body of learning. They laugh at him. To grant his corrections would be to publish their own mistakes, and their reputations will not carry it. A modern gloss ties this rebuff to the alumbrados, a Spanish mystical movement that does not exist until the 1500s, a full century after the date the legend gives, and the contradiction is left standing here rather than smoothed. He tries other nations. It goes no better, and the Fama names none of them.
suggested_refs: Toledo, proposed by tradition; the alumbrados association, anachronistic by a century
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

segments.name: The House of the Holy Spirit

stops.name: Germany, a fitting and neat habitation
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama gives the return and the building with no year attached
stops.campa: He returns into Germany, a country he loves, the Fama says, for the alterations and the strange and dangerous contentions shortly to come upon it. The sentence is written in 1614 about a man dated to 1400 and it points at the Reformation. He builds himself a fitting and neat habitation and shuts the door. For five years he writes down what he learned, works his mathematical instruments, and speaks to no one about a fraternity. The town is never named. It is the same unlocated Germany that raised him and will bury him.
stops.quote: returned again into Germany, the which he (by reason of the alterations which were shortly to come, and of the strange and dangerous contentions) heartily loved
suggested_refs: The unnamed German habitation, later the site of Sancti Spiritus and of the vault
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Germany, five years, then three cloister-brethren
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Fama's five years run from the return, not from the start of his travels; the absolute year is arithmetic
stops.campa: After five years the wished for reformation comes again into his mind. He does not seek it among the learned who laughed at him; he sends to his first cloister, the poor house that taught him Greek and Latin, and calls out three men he knew there as a boy: G.V., I.A., I.O. The four of them build a magical language and a dictionary the brethren say is still in daily use. The order begins with four persons only, not eight. Everything the manifesto claims for it is built by men who were educated by charity.
stops.quote: After this manner began the Fraternity of the Rosie Cross; first, by four persons onely
suggested_refs: The magical language and dictionary of the first four brethren, described but never reproduced
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Sancti Spiritus, the house finished and the six articles sworn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1407 appears nowhere in the Fama and is a later arithmetic figure widely repeated as if textual
stops.campa: The new building is finished and they call it Sancti Spiritus, the House of the Holy Spirit. Four more are admitted, the founder's kinsman R.C., a painter called B., and G. and P.D. who serves as secretary, so that in all they are eight. They bind themselves by six articles: to profess nothing but to cure the sick, and that gratis; to wear no habit that marks them out; to meet every year at the House; each to name his successor; the word R.C. for their seal and character; and the Fraternity to stay secret one hundred years.
stops.quote: his new building (called Sancti Spiritus) was now finished
suggested_refs: The six articles of the Fraternity, the order's whole constitution as the Fama gives it
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Sancti Spiritus, the brethren scatter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Fama gives no date for the dispersal at all; the widely cited 1410 is invented and 1408 here is placeholder ordering only
stops.campa: Five of the brethren depart to different countries, to practise the cure gratis and to gather what each country knows. B. and D. remain a whole year with the father and then go too, and after that only his kinsman C.O. is with him, so that he has two of his brethren by him all the days of his life. No year is given for any of this. The founder who was received in Arabia as one long expected spends his old age in an unnamed German house with a cousin, waiting on an annual return the text never describes.
stops.quote: five of the Brethren departed, only the Brethren B. and D. remained with the Father Fra. R. C. a whole year
suggested_refs: The yearly reconvening at Sancti Spiritus, stipulated in the articles and never narrated
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Framlingham, the young Earl of Norfolk cured
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama gives country and title, no town and no year; the pin is a reasoned guess at the earldom's seat
stops.campa: One of the eight is much spoken of in England, chiefly because he cured a young Earl of Norfolk of the leprosy, without fee, as the article requires. The Fama gives the country and the title and no town. Framlingham Castle carries the pin because it was the seat of the Bigod earls and later of the Mowbray and Howard dukes of Norfolk, which puts the likeliest hall for the story in Suffolk rather than in the county the title names. The order's only recorded act outside Germany is a healing in England.
stops.quote: In England he is much spoken of, and chiefly because he cured a young Earl of Norfolk of the Leprosie
suggested_refs: Framlingham Castle, Suffolk, seat of the Bigod earls and the Howard dukes of Norfolk
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

segments.name: The Grave Kept From the Order

stops.name: Germany, dead past a hundred years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1484 is arithmetic from the Confessio alone, 1378 plus 106; the Fama gives no year and says only centenario major
stops.campa: He dies past a hundred years old. The Confessio counts the years, one hundred six of them from 1378, which is arithmetic anyone can run to 1484; the Fama's Latin elogium says only centenario major and insists on the manner rather than the sum, that no sickness had ever touched his body and that God's spirit called the illuminated soul out of it. He does not die of anything. In the canon this is a technical statement about what the medicine of Damcar and Fez actually did, and not a compliment.
stops.quote: these one hundred six years of his life, which he hath left to our Brethren and us after his decease to peruse
suggested_refs: The Latin Elogium of the Fama, which gives the manner of death and withholds the number

stops.name: Germany, the burial none of the next generation knows
stops.date_confidence: legendary: the Fama states the concealment and gives no date; the month is a default
stops.campa: The brethren bury him, and they do not tell anyone where. Not the next generation of the order, not the eight who succeed the eight; the location is a blank kept from the inside. For a hundred and twenty years the Fraternity meets yearly at the House of the Holy Spirit and passes down every article except this one. The grave is inside the building they use. They do not know it, and the manifesto is explicit that they do not know it, which is what makes the finding a discovery and not a visit.
suggested_refs: The concealed sepulchre of the founder, unlocated in both manifestos
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: The Fraternity's building, the nail and the memorial table
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1604 is arithmetic, 1484 plus 120; the Fama's own wording about where the interval begins is inexact
stops.campa: A brother is altering part of the building, meaning to move the memorial table to a better vault. In the table sticks a great nail, strong; drawn out with force it brings away an indifferent big stone out of the thin wall, and behind the plaster is a door. Over the door, in great letters: Post 120 annos patebo. After 120 years I shall open. The brethren wait until morning, and they count. The founder buried in secret has left the hour of his own uncovering in the masonry, and the masonry has kept it.
stops.quote: In this Table stuck a great naile somewhat strong; so that when he was with force drawn out, he took with him an indifferent big stone out of the thin wall
suggested_refs: The memorial table and the door inscribed Post CXX Annos Patebo
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: The vault of seven sides
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: same 120-year arithmetic; the day is sequencing only, the Fama gives no calendar date
stops.campa: A vault of seven sides and corners, every side five foot broad, and the height of eight foot. No window and no natural light, and it is lit anyway from a sun set in the ceiling, divided by the seven sides with a bright triangle at its centre. The floor is parted in the triangle and shows the power and rule of the inferior governors. Every one of the seven walls has a door for a chest, and in the chests are the books of the order, looking-glasses of divers virtues, little bells, and burning lamps still burning.
stops.quote: a Vault of seven sides and corners, every side five foot broad, and the height of eight foot
suggested_refs: The heptagonal vault, later rebuilt as stage furniture by the Golden Dawn
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: The round altar and its three inscriptions
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sequencing within the discovery; no calendar date exists in the text
stops.campa: On the round altar in the middle, plated in brass: A. C. R. C. Hoc universi compendium unius mihi sepulchrum feci. I made this compendium of the universe my own sepulchre. Round the first circle or brim stands Jesus mihi omnia. In the middle, four figures circumscribed Nequaquam vacuum, Legis Jugum, Libertas Evangelii, Dei gloria intacta. Three positions, not one inscription; the summaries that run them into a single Latin sentence and reorder the last three are compressing a room into a line.
stops.quote: A. C. R. C. Hoc universi compendium unius mihi sepulchrum feci
suggested_refs: The altar plate, the brim inscription, and the four circumscribed figures, three distinct positions in the vault
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: The vault, the body whole and the book called I
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sequencing within the discovery; no calendar date exists in the text
stops.campa: Under the altar they lift a plate of brass and find a fair and worthy body, whole and unconsumed, holding a parchment book in its hand. The book is lettered I in Vaughan's English; other editions read T, and the corpus does not choose between them. The body is the founder. A hundred and twenty years in a sealed room have done nothing to it, exactly as the article about curing the sick gratis implied and never said. They read the book, they close the vault, and they tell Europe about it ten years later.
stops.quote: in his hand he held a parchment book, Called I.
suggested_refs: The parchment book of the vault, read I in Vaughan and T in other editions
sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614), trans. Thomas Vaughan, 1652, Wikisource

stops.name: Herrenberg, birth of Johann Valentin Andreae
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Johann Valentin Andreae is born at Herrenberg in the Duchy of Wurttemberg, a hundred and two years after Christian Rosenkreuz is said to have died. He will write, as a young man around 1605, a seven day allegorical romance in which an old C.R. is summoned by a flying letter to a royal wedding. He will later call it a ludibrium, a jest, and in old age present himself as an orthodox Lutheran who had nothing at all to do with the two manifestos. That is a distancing. It is not a documented denial of authorship.
suggested_refs: Andreae's autobiography and the composition of the Chymical Wedding, c.1605

stops.name: Tyrol, Haselmayer reads a manuscript Fama
stops.date_confidence: attested for the manuscript circulation; month and day default to 01-01
stops.campa: A manuscript of the Fama is circulating in the Tyrol. Adam Haselmayer has read a copy by 1610 and publishes a reply to it in 1612, before any printer has set the text. The order's own announcement reaches its first known reader in handwriting, passed between people who could not have bought it. Whether an imprint of 1610 ever existed is a separate question and the answer is no: 1610 is the date of the manuscript, and the loose phrasing that turns it into a Kassel printing is a modern error carried forward without checking.
suggested_refs: Adam Haselmayer's 1612 published reply to a manuscript Fama

stops.name: Kassel, the Fama Fraternitatis printed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day default to 01-01
stops.campa: The Fama Fraternitatis is printed at Kassel by Wilhelm Wessel, bound into the Allgemeine und General Reformation, which is itself a German translation of the seventy seventh ragguaglio of Trajano Boccalini, Venice 1612. The order's manifesto arrives in the world as an appendix to an Italian satire. It claims to report a real fraternity's real history and names no author. Francis Bacon's file in this atlas carries the persistent unproven tradition that he was the guiding hand behind these pages, and Kassel is where that tradition points.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine und General Reformation der gantzen weiten Welt, Kassel: Wilhelm Wessel, 1614

stops.name: Kassel, the Confessio Fraternitatis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the city; the Frankfurt reading in one Wikipedia article is an error there, not a live dispute
stops.campa: A second manifesto follows from the same city a year later, sharper, in Latin, appended to Philip a Gabella's Secretioris Philosophiae Consideratio Brevis. It supplies the two numbers the Fama never gives: the year 1378, in which our Christian Father was born, and the one hundred six years of his life. Everything datable about Christian Rosenkreuz comes from this pamphlet. It also spells the sages' city Damear, which is not what the Fama's English spells, and neither text was ever brought into line with the other.
suggested_refs: Philip a Gabella, Secretioris Philosophiae Consideratio Brevis, Kassel 1615, with the Latin Confessio appended

stops.name: Leiden, Fludd's apology for a fraternity he never met
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the common attribution of Fludd's defences to England is wrong, both were printed at Leiden
stops.campa: Robert Fludd, an English physician who has never met a Rosicrucian, publishes at Leiden a compendious apology for the Fraternity, and follows it the next year with a longer tract. He is defending an order that has issued two pamphlets and no address, against critics who have exactly the same information he does. Fludd stands in this atlas's queue beside John Dee, Paracelsus and this journey, named there as a designed cluster; the Fama's answer to him and to everyone else is that the brethren will find those they want.
suggested_refs: Robert Fludd, Apologia Compendiaria (Leiden 1616) and Tractatus Apologeticus (Leiden 1617)

stops.name: Strasbourg, the Chymical Wedding
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and city; the month is a default placing it after Fludd's Leiden apology
stops.campa: The third book appears at Strasbourg, printed by Lazarus Zetzner and dated in its title to the year 1459: the Chymische Hochzeit. It is not a manifesto. It is a romance in seven days, in the first person, in which an old man is called by a winged letter to a wedding at a castle, weighed on a scale against virtues, and set to work at an alchemical resurrection with a company that keeps dying. Its geography is symbolic from end to end; no road, mountain or gate in it has been matched to a place on any map.
stops.quote: It was an Evening before Easter-Day, I sate at a Table, and having (as my Custom was) in my humble Prayer sufficiently conversed with my Creator, and considered many great Mysteries
stops.quote_source: Chymische Hochzeit, First Day, in the English of E. Foxcroft, 'The Hermetick Romance, or, The Chymical Wedding' (London: A. Sowle, 1690); note the year 1459 appears in the German title, not in this opening sentence
suggested_refs: Chymische Hochzeit: Christiani Rosencreutz. Anno 1459, Strasbourg: Lazarus Zetzner, 1616
sources: E. Foxcroft trans., The Hermetick Romance (1690), archive.org item hermetickromance00rose

stops.name: Tubingen, the ludibrium
stops.date_confidence: attested for Menippus 1617; the same label recurs in Turris Babel 1619
stops.campa: Andreae, educated and later active around Tubingen, calls the Chymical Wedding a ludibrium in Menippus, and calls it that again in Turris Babel two years on. The word covers a range: jest, game, plaything, a thing set up in order to be knocked down. He is a Lutheran pastor by now with a career to protect and a Europe full of pamphleteers claiming his story as fact. Whether Christian Rosenkreuz existed as a legend before this circle wrote him, or is their fiction fitted afterwards with a genealogy, is the question the manifestos leave standing.
suggested_refs: Andreae, Menippus (1617) and Turris Babel (1619)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Maier's Themis Aurea
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; Maier was at Frankfurt from 1616 and moved to Magdeburg in 1620
stops.campa: Michael Maier, once physician to Rudolf II, publishes at Frankfurt Silentium post clamores and then Themis Aurea, laying out the laws of a Fraternity he also never found. Maier does not read the alchemy as metaphor; he remains an operative alchemist, and the tidy claim that the defenders spiritualised the work into pure symbol does not fit him. Between the manifestos and 1620 some four hundred books and pamphlets are printed for and against the order. Not one of them produces a member.
suggested_refs: Michael Maier, Silentium post clamores (1617) and Themis Aurea (1618)

stops.name: Paris, the posters of the Deputies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day default to 01-01
stops.campa: Posters appear on the walls of Paris announcing the Deputies of the Higher College of the Rose Croix, present in the city visibly and invisibly. The city takes fright. Nobody knows who put them up and nobody produces a Deputy. Eight years after Kassel the legend has crossed a language and a border and turned from a report about a dead German into an anonymous claim about a living presence in a capital. The order is being read off a wall by people who have never opened the pamphlets.
suggested_refs: The 1622 Paris placards of the Rose-Croix and the pamphlet panic that followed

segments.name: The Orders That Take His Name

stops.name: London, Vaughan's Fame and Confession
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day default to 01-01
stops.campa: Thomas Vaughan, writing as Eugenius Philalethes, publishes at London the first English Fame and Confession of the Fraternity of R.C., thirty eight years after Kassel. Every phrase this journey quotes comes through his hand: the fifth year of age, the wise received him not as a stranger, Post 120 annos patebo, the vault of seven sides. What the English speaking world has argued over for four centuries is a Welsh alchemist's translation of an anonymous German pamphlet about a man who has no birthplace.
suggested_refs: The Fame and Confession of the Fraternity of R.C., London 1652, the source text for every English quotation in this journey
sources: Wikisource, The Fame and Confession of the Fraternity of R.C.

stops.name: Germany, Sincerus Renatus and the Golden and Rosy Cross
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1710 book; the order it anticipates dates to the 1750s, so the common claim that 1710 founds it is wrong
stops.campa: A book by Sigmund Richter, writing as Sincerus Renatus, sets out the rules of a Gold und Rosenkreuz brotherhood. The order that takes the name will not exist for another forty years; the book anticipates it rather than founds it. In 1785 that order prints the Geheime Figuren, the secret symbols of the Rosicrucians of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, plates of a tradition it dates to a century before its own founding. The founder's own method, an order remembered backwards into existence, is now being applied to the founder.
suggested_refs: Sincerus Renatus, Die wahrhaffte und vollkommene Bereitung des Philosophischen Steins (1710); Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (1785)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross'

stops.name: Aldermanbury, the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia
stops.date_confidence: attested: the formation meeting is 1 June 1867; the 1865 date in wide circulation belongs to Little's obtaining the rituals
stops.campa: The Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia holds its formation meeting at Aldermanbury in the City of London, with Robert Wentworth Little elected Master Magus. This pin is the atlas's canonical Rosicrucian address, inherited byte for byte from Bulwer-Lytton's file and used again in Theodor Reuss's. Freemasons only, Christians only, nine grades. The vault in the unnamed German house has become a set of degrees conferred in a London street, and the street has a number.
suggested_refs: Aldermanbury, City of London; pin inherited from bulwer_lytton.journey.json and theodor_reuss.journey.json

stops.name: London, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1887 founding; the frequently given 1888 is the founding of the Isis-Urania temple, a different event
stops.campa: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn is founded in London by Westcott, Woodman and Mathers out of the Cipher Manuscripts decoded that year; the Isis-Urania temple follows in 1888, and the two dates get merged in most accounts. Its grade structure descends from the Gold und Rosenkreuz through the SRIA, and its Adeptus Minor ceremony seats the candidate in a built replica of the seven sided vault, with the Chief Adept lying in the tomb as Christian Rosenkreuz. The room in the Fama is now furniture, assembled and struck.
suggested_refs: The Cipher Manuscripts and the Vault of the Adepti, a built reconstruction of the Fama's heptagonal chamber
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn'

stops.name: Aldermanbury, Westcott's charter to Theodor Reuss
stops.date_confidence: attested, per theodor_reuss.journey.json
stops.campa: Theodor Reuss receives a Rosicrucian charter from W. W. Westcott, Supreme Magus of the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, at this same Aldermanbury address. Reuss will use it, with the other warrants he collects, to assemble the Ordo Templi Orientis; he will charter Rudolf Steiner for a Berlin chapter called Mystica Aeterna, and send a gauge of amity to H. Spencer Lewis in California. Authority in this line travels by paper, and the earliest sheet in the chain is a pamphlet nobody signed.
suggested_refs: The Westcott charter of 26 July 1901, foundation document of Reuss's Rosicrucian claim

stops.name: Seattle, the Rosicrucian Fellowship founded
stops.date_confidence: attested: 8 August 1909 at Seattle; the Oceanside, California founding given in many sources conflates this with the 1911 opening of Mount Ecclesia
stops.campa: Max Heindel founds the Rosicrucian Fellowship at Seattle on the eighth of August, teaching Christian Rosenkreuz as a living initiate and the order as a real body of thirteen. Mount Ecclesia at Oceanside in California, which most accounts give as the founding place, is not opened until 1911 and its temple not dedicated until 1920. Heindel also holds, with Rudolf Steiner, that the founder returned in the person of the Count of Saint Germain, dead in 1784. The 106 years the Confessio counted are no longer a lifespan; they are one visit.
suggested_refs: Mount Ecclesia, Oceanside, opened 1911, temple dedicated 1920

stops.name: Munich, The Portal of Initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested, per steiner.journey.json
stops.campa: Rudolf Steiner stages The Portal of Initiation at the Schauspielhaus in Munich, billed as a Rosicrucian mystery through Rudolf Steiner. He has already carried what he calls the Rosicrucian stream, the Christ centred West, into the Theosophical Society at London in 1902, and revived its imagery at the Munich congress of 1907; he holds a Deputy Grand Master's warrant from Reuss for a Berlin chapter he has stripped of its sexual material. It is played in a public theatre, to an audience that bought tickets.
suggested_refs: Die Pforte der Einweihung, Schauspielhaus, Munich, 15 August 1910

stops.name: Sintra, the Well of Initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1904-1910 construction; the Rosicrucian reading of the site is a later and contested interpretation
stops.campa: At Sintra, Carvalho Monteiro and the architect Luigi Manini finish the Quinta da Regaleira: a garden with an inverted tower sunk into the hillside, landings spiralling down to a floor laid with a rose of the winds on a Templar cross. Later commentators read the Well of Initiation as a Rosicrucian descent and the whole estate as a Rosenkreuz monument. The reading is contested and the building is real, which reverses the founder's case exactly: here the vault exists and the doctrine attached to it is the invention.
suggested_refs: The Poco Iniciatico of the Quinta da Regaleira, Sintra, built 1904-1910

stops.name: California, the Ancient Mystical Order Rosae Crucis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1915 incorporation in the United States; the pool names no city for it, and California enters through theodor_reuss.journey.json and the order's later seat at San Jose
stops.campa: H. Spencer Lewis incorporates the Ancient Mystical Order Rosae Crucis, claiming a lineage running from Egypt through the Fama's fraternity to himself; the order will seat itself in California, where Theodor Reuss's file records a gauge of amity sent to Lewis late in Reuss's life. Five centuries after a boy is placed in a cloister in the fifth year of his age, in a Germany with no name, the fraternity he is said to have founded is a corporation with a mailing address. No verifiable record confirms that he existed.
suggested_refs: The AMORC Rosicrucian Park and Egyptian Museum, San Jose, California, the order's later seat
